title: Corgi Insurance Reaches $4 Billion Valuation With Third Raise in Three Months
excerpt: The Y Combinator-backed AI insurtech has tripled its valuation since May, though the latest round's size and investors remain undisclosed.
body:
• Forbes reported that Corgi closed another Series B extension at a $4 billion valuation, its third funding round since May 2026.
  • The company projects its revenue run rate will grow from $45 million at the start of 2026 to $450 million by year-end — a tenfold increase.
  • The rapid-fire fundraising has drawn scrutiny from limited partners concerned about internal markups by existing investors.

Corgi Closes Third Round in Under Three Months

Insurance technology startup Corgi has closed yet another funding round, this time at a $4 billion valuation, according to a Forbes report published on July 22. The raise marks the company's third in under three months, capping a fundraising blitz that has taken the San Francisco-based startup from unicorn status to one of the most highly valued private insurtechs in the United States.

Neither the amount raised nor the participating investors were disclosed. A Corgi spokesperson declined to confirm the round to Forbes.

The latest extension follows a $160 million Series B in May that valued Corgi at $1.3 billion, and a $106 million Series B1 in late May that doubled its valuation to $2.6 billion. Prior to those rounds, the company had raised $108 million across its seed and Series A at a $630 million valuation in January 2026. Total disclosed funding stands at $378 million.

Revenue Trajectory Driving Investor Interest

Corgi is projecting that its revenue run rate will surge from $45 million at the beginning of 2026 to $450 million by year-end, according to Forbes. The company had around $100 million in annualized revenue as of its Series B1 in late May, and CEO Nico Laqua said at the time that the company had been profitable in the prior month.

"Commercial insurance infrastructure has historically been slow, manual, and difficult for operators to navigate."

— Nico Laqua, Co-founder and CEO, Corgi

Founded in 2024 by Laqua and Emily Yuan, Corgi emerged from Y Combinator's Summer 2024 batch and received regulatory approval to operate as a licensed insurance carrier in July 2025. Unlike most insurtech startups that sit atop legacy carriers and earn a cut of premiums, Corgi operates as a full-stack carrier — handling underwriting, policy management, and claims end-to-end on its own infrastructure.

The company's product lines include directors and officers liability, cyber insurance, commercial general liability, and AI liability coverage. Its client roster includes workforce management platform Deel and AI sales startup Artisan.

Rapid Expansion Into New Verticals

Corgi has been moving aggressively beyond its startup insurance roots. In July 2026, the company launched a dedicated trucking insurance division and unveiled "Golden by Corgi," a vertical focused on the sports and entertainment sector. It is also expanding into small business insurance.

The company is headquartered in San Francisco's Financial District, where it operates a 24/7 café on the ground floor of its offices. It has additional offices in Salt Lake City, Atlanta, Chicago, Dallas, New York, and London.

LP Scrutiny Over Back-to-Back Markups

Corgi's fundraising cadence — three rounds in under three months, each from largely the same investor base led by growth equity firm TCV — has drawn attention in venture capital circles. The practice of existing investors repricing a company upward in quick succession can inflate paper returns without a liquidity event.

"There's growing distrust of internal markups. If a company is just getting re-priced upward with no real liquidity event, LPs notice."

— An unnamed limited partner, via TechCrunch

Kanyi Maqubela of Kindred Ventures, a Corgi investor, pushed back on that concern, telling TechCrunch that "LPs really like exits above all" and that "revenue growth rationalized the new round." The distinction between an upmark led by existing investors and a competitive repricing by a new outside lead remains a live debate in LP circles.

What's Next

With a $4 billion valuation and an aggressive revenue target, Corgi faces pressure to deliver on its projections. The tenfold revenue jump it is forecasting for 2026 would be extraordinary even by the standards of the current AI boom. Whether Corgi can sustain that trajectory — and eventually convert paper markups into real liquidity for its backers — will determine if the company's rapid ascent holds up under scrutiny.

The broader insurtech sector will be watching closely. If Corgi's full-stack carrier model proves out, it could reshape how commercial insurance is underwritten and distributed. If the growth stalls, it may become a cautionary tale about the risks of velocity-driven fundraising in a frothy market.
